title: Trees & BST
tagline: DFS recursion, BFS layer traversal, and the BST invariant that makes search, insert, delete all O(log n).
intro:
A tree is a hierarchy of **nodes**, each with a value and links to its children; a binary tree limits that to a left and right child. Trees are where recursion pays off most: nearly every tree problem is solved by the same move — *do something with the current node, then recurse into the children and combine* — because a tree is literally defined in terms of smaller trees.

The star of this module is the **binary search tree (BST)**: a binary tree with one invariant — everything in the left subtree is smaller, everything in the right is larger. That single rule turns search, insert, and delete into O(log n) operations on a balanced tree, and makes an in-order traversal spit out values in sorted order.

This module covers the traversal orders (and what each is good for), the DFS recursion template, BFS level-order, lowest common ancestor, and the BST operations — with the complexity caveat that an unbalanced tree degrades everything to O(n).
objectives: Traverse a tree preorder, inorder, postorder (DFS) and level-order (BFS)
Write the universal DFS recursion template for tree problems
Exploit the BST invariant for O(log n) search, insert, and validation
Know why inorder traversal of a BST yields sorted order
Find the lowest common ancestor in a general tree and a BST
Explain how balance affects complexity (O(log n) balanced vs O(n) skewed)

signals: Hierarchical/nested data: file systems, org charts, expression trees
"Traverse / sum / find depth / check balance" of a tree
Sorted data with frequent insert/delete and order queries → BST
Shortest path / level-by-level → BFS on the tree
antiSignals: Need O(1) lookup by key without order → hash map
Graph with cycles → graph algorithms (trees are acyclic)

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
A tree is like an org chart: one boss at the top, and each person has a few people reporting below them. A binary search tree adds one tidy rule - smaller values go left, bigger values go right - so finding something becomes a guided search that drops half the remaining people at every step.

Example: in a binary search tree, reading the nodes in the order left-then-node-then-right (called an inorder walk) spits everyone out already sorted, for free. So a question like 'find the 3rd smallest value' turns into 'walk inorder and stop at the 3rd one' - no sorting step needed, because the tree's shape already encodes the order.

sections.heading: Tree vocabulary
sections.body:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Root** | The top node, no parent |
| **Leaf** | A node with no children |
| **Height** | Longest root-to-leaf edge count |
| **Depth** | Edges from the root to a given node |
| **Balanced** | Left/right heights differ by ≤ 1 everywhere → O(log n) height |
| **BST invariant** | left subtree < node < right subtree, recursively |
| **Complete** | All levels full except possibly the last, filled left-to-right (heaps) |

The word **balanced** is doing heavy lifting: a balanced binary tree has height ~log n, so traversing a root-to-leaf path is O(log n). A degenerate (skewed) tree is really a linked list with height n.

sections.heading: The four traversals and when to use each
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R["node"] --> L["left subtree"]
  R --> RT["right subtree"]
```

DFS visits a whole branch before backtracking; the three DFS orders differ only in *when* you process the current node relative to its children.

| Traversal | Order | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Preorder** | node, left, right | copy/serialize a tree, prefix expressions |
| **Inorder** | left, node, right | **BST → sorted output**, kth smallest |
| **Postorder** | left, right, node | delete/free a tree, compute heights, bottom-up DP |
| **Level-order (BFS)** | level by level | shortest path, level sums, right-side view |

Memorise: **inorder of a BST is sorted.** That fact alone solves 'kth smallest', 'validate BST', and 'two-sum in BST'.

sections.heading: The universal DFS template
sections.body: Almost every tree problem fits one recursive shape: handle the empty (null) base case, recurse left and right, then combine. Whether you're computing depth, summing values, or checking balance, only the 'combine' step changes.

codeExamples.label: Max depth (postorder combine)
Inorder traversal (BST -> sorted)
codeExamples.code:
def inorder(root, out):
    if not root:
        return
    inorder(root.left, out)   # left
    out.append(root.val)      # node
    inorder(root.right, out)  # right
    # for a BST, `out` is now sorted

sections.heading: BFS level-order on trees
sections.body: Use a queue and process one level at a time by snapshotting the queue size before each level loop. BFS is the natural fit for anything 'per level': level averages, right-side view (last node of each level), minimum depth, and zigzag traversal.

sections.heading: BST operations and the invariant
sections.body: The BST invariant lets you discard half the tree at each step, exactly like binary search. To **search**, go left if the target is smaller, right if larger. **Insert** follows the same path to the empty slot. **Validate** by checking that every node lies within an inherited (min, max) range — not just that its immediate children compare correctly.

codeExamples.label: Validate a BST with min/max bounds

callouts.text: Validating a BST by only comparing a node to its direct children is WRONG — a deep descendant can violate the invariant. Pass down (min, max) bounds, or do an inorder traversal and check it's strictly increasing.

sections.heading: Lowest common ancestor
sections.body: The LCA of two nodes is the deepest node that has both as descendants. In a **general binary tree**, recurse: if the current node is one of the targets, return it; otherwise look left and right — if both sides return non-null, the current node is the LCA. In a **BST**, it's even easier: walk down, and the LCA is the first node whose value lies *between* the two targets (the split point).

callouts.text: For a BST LCA, you don't need to search both subtrees: if both targets are smaller, go left; both larger, go right; otherwise this node is the split point and the LCA. O(log n) on a balanced tree.

interviewTalking: State the traversal you'll use and why: "This needs bottom-up information — a child's height before the parent's — so I'll use postorder DFS." For BST problems, invoke the invariant: "Because left < node < right, I can binary-search the tree, and an inorder traversal gives me sorted order for free." Always give complexity in terms of balance: "O(h) where h is the height — O(log n) if balanced, O(n) worst case if the tree is skewed."
commonMistakes: Validating a BST by comparing only to immediate children instead of inherited min/max bounds
Forgetting the null base case in tree recursion → NullPointerException
Quoting O(log n) for BST ops without noting it degrades to O(n) on a skewed tree
Not snapshotting queue size in BFS, so levels bleed together
Confusing height (down to leaf) with depth (down from root)
Using preorder when the problem needs bottom-up (postorder) information
complexityNotes: Tree traversals (DFS or BFS) are O(n) time visiting every node, with O(h) space for the recursion stack / O(w) for the BFS queue (h = height, w = max width). BST search/insert/delete are O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst case when skewed.
